evidence.note: Non-US origin work (France). URAA (17 USC 104A) restores copyright only for the 'remainder of the term the work would otherwise have been granted.' For a 1919 French publication, the maximum theoretical US term with all extensions (28-year initial + 47-year extended renewal under 1976 Act + 20-year CTEA) would have expired circa 2014. Even a hypothetical URAA restoration would itself be exhausted by 2026. No ongoing protection survives.

editorial:
J'accuse! (1919) is an anti-war silent epic written and directed by Abel Gance and produced by PathÃ© FrÃ¨res during the final year of World War I. Its most famous sequenceâ€”the dead of the trenches rising to indict the livingâ€”was filmed using actual French soldiers temporarily withdrawn from the Verdun sector; a number of those men were killed in action before the film reached theaters. The US cut, retitled I Accuse, was released in 1921 through United Artists after D.W. Griffith arranged distribution following a private New York screening attended by Griffith and Lillian Gish; that version softened the pacifist framing and appended a reconciliatory ending.

The underlying 1919 print is in US public domain by term exhaustion: the maximum US copyright term for a 1919 publicationâ€”including a hypothetical URAA restoration for a French work plus CTEA extensionsâ€”expired no later than 2014, leaving the images unencumbered as of 2026. The concrete rights trap is the 2008 Lobster Films/Nederlands Filmmuseum reconstruction, released on DVD by Flicker Alley with a new score composed by Robert Israel. That specific digital master and its accompanying score are separately copyrighted. Creators should source a print from Archive.org uploads independent of the Lobster/Flicker Alley master and must compose or license their own musical accompaniment for any presentation.
faq: Is the 1919 J'accuse! print free to use in the US?

The original silent print is in US public domain by term expiryâ€”no renewal or URAA issue survives to 2026. Two things remain encumbered: the Robert Israel score on the 2008 Flicker Alley DVD (a new composition with its own copyright) and the specific Lobster Films digital restoration master. Use a PD-sourced Archive.org print with your own audio to stay clear of both.
Does the 1921 US release I Accuse create a separate copyright problem?

No. Even if United Artists registered a separate US copyright on the 1921 cut and it was subsequently renewed, the maximum CTEA-extended term for a 1921 copyright expired on January 1, 2017. That version is also in US public domain as of 2026.
